They did comp to the two factor model. His difference between 1 and 10 was 17% and the difference for the two factor model was 5 percent and change. That was very powerful. His worst 36 month period was minus 40% and the two factor model was plus 14%. So I thought that was good.

## 投资组合管理

<!--en-->
*Portfolio Management*

我也简要谈到了投资组合管理，因此我认为我们现在也该稍微讨论一下。

<!--en-->
I also talked a little about Portfolio Management so I also think we should talk about that a little bit now.

当你们从这儿（哥伦比亚大学商学院）毕业之后，可能会面临以下困难：

<!--en-->
When you guys get out of here (Columbia Graduate Business School) it might be difficult to:

A. 拥有持有5到8只股票的信心；B. 找到愿意支持你这么做的人。我想在以下场合你能做到这一点：

<!--en-->
A. have the confidence to own 5 to 8 stocks and
B. Have someone who is crazy enough to let you do that.
I imagine you can do that in:

哥伦比亚大学商学院的特殊情况投资课程中：A. 在你的个人账户里；B. 在你能够掌控局面的地方。有人主张应构建*高度集中的投资组合*。实际上，你就是在购买企业的部分所有权。在我看来，应将其视为自己的生意——你持有那些经过充分研究并以折价买入的优秀企业的股份。如果你能以50或60美分的价格买到它们，就不会整天担心市价波动了。

<!--en-->
Special Situation Investing Classes at Columbia University Business School
A. your personal account and
B. where you have control over things
There is an argument to have a *very concentrated portfolio*. You really are buying pieces of the business. The way I look at it. Think about it as your own business where you own percentages of other good businesses that you researched well and bought at a discount. And if you can buy it for 50 or 60 cents on the dollar you wouldn't worry about where people were pricing it all day long.

传统MBA课程中教授的投资组合管理方法，在此看来会显得*可笑至极*。机构业务中会发生什么？当它们把钱交给基金经理时，并不会深入查看投资组合细节（比如养老基金经理并不清楚基金经理为何选择特定股票）。他们缺乏透明度，既不知道你为何买入这些股票，也只看到你的收益起伏不定。如果仅凭数字来判断——我理解这个过程可能需要三年以上才能见效。如果你的业绩不佳，我为何要选你呢？这有点像*沃伦·E·巴菲特（WEB）*说的：“我寻找的是身高7英尺的篮球运动员。”

<!--en-->
All the measurements you would get in a traditional MBA in how to do portfolio management would look *silly*. What happens in the institutional business? When they put out money to money managers, they don't go inside the portfolio (the pension fund managers, for example, don't know the reason why those particular stocks were purchased by the fund manager). They don't have transparency, they don't know why you bought those stocks, and they only know that your returns bounce around. If that is all you have-just the numbers-I understand the process could take longer than three years to work out. If your numbers are no good why should I pick you? Sort of like *Warren E. Buffett (WEB)* "I look for 7 foot basketball players."

道理类似：如果某人三年表现不佳，你就该抛弃他，转而选择表现优异的人。如果现在行不通，将来又怎会奏效呢？

<!--en-->
It is sort of the same concept. If someone has not done well for three years, you should ditch them to go with people who have done well. If it is not working well now, then why will it work now or in the future?

我参与一些机构的（投资）董事会，这就是他们的思路。这正是*妙处所在*。那些三年表现不佳的人不得不卖掉所有持仓，因为资金被抽走——导致股价进一步下跌。（*讽刺的是，这通常发生在业绩反转前夕*）。从中可见机构层面的原因。

<!--en-->
I am on some institutional (investment) boards and that is the thinking. That is the *great thing*. The guy, who doesn't do well over three years, so he has to sell all his stuff because his money is pulled—so his stocks get even cheaper. (*Ironically usually just before the turnaround*). You can see the institutional reason why this does happen.

最好的例子是：年度波动率与十年波动率大致与市场持平。以过去36个月为周期，*Pzena*的波动率约为市场的一半。我并不特别推崇这两种（波动率衡量方式）。

<!--en-->
The best example, annual volatility then 10 year volatility, it is about equal to the market. Using trailing 36 months periods, *Pzena's* volatility is about *half* the markets' volatility. I am not a big proponent of either (*measuring volatility*).

如果回报可观，谁会在意期间波动有多大呢？看看统计数据：一年中你的回撤幅度是多少？当你以合理价格持有一家企业的股份时，所有这些指标似乎都显得有些可笑。

<!--en-->
Who cares how much it bounces around in the interim if returns are good? If you look at the statistics what are your draw downs during the course of the year? All of those measures seem a little silly when *you own a share of a business at a good price*.

**学生：** 过去二十年里，你最希望自己能有所不同的一点是什么？你最常犯的错误是什么？

<!--en-->
**Student:** What was the one mistake over the past twenty years, you wish you did a little bit differently? What was your most common mistake?

**JG：** 我告诉你一件*令人鼓舞的事*：我犯过很多愚蠢的错误，我不愿提及，而且还没完——这会勾起不快的情绪。我曾过早且错误地卖出股票。不过，只要你做对足够多的事，仍能获得丰厚回报，我觉得这很鼓舞人心。相信我，若回顾过去30年的错误——实在令人尴尬——但我确实曾以25美分的价格卖出一只如今价值15美元的股票。**卖出它毫无逻辑可言。**当时我正在筹款，能筹到多少呢？如果你知道我犯了多少错……不仅仅是*过早卖出*，尽管这是我们经常犯的错误。

<!--en-->
**JG:** I will tell you something *encouraging*, I have done so many stupid things, and I hate to talk about them and I am not done—it brings up bad emotions. I have sold too soon and at wrong times. Yet, if you do enough stuff right you can still get great returns, I think that is encouraging. Believe me If I go back over the past 30 years and recount my mistakes—it is too embarrassing—but I did sell a stock at 25 cents that is now $15. **There was no logic to selling it.** I was raising money. How much could I raise? If you knew how many mistakes I have made......not just *selling too early* though that is one that we often do.

我记得我和合伙人*罗伯特·戈德斯坦*有过一次较量。我们在*穆迪公司*的投资上赚了60%到70%，结果完全如我们所料，但该头寸的价值甚至翻了三倍。我们为此争论了30分钟。那些我们卖出后价格翻三倍的股票呢？这无疑是我们的一个错误，而且还在继续犯。

<!--en-->
I think I had a contest with *Robert Goldstein*, my partner. We made 60% to 70% on our money with *Moody's* and it unfolded exactly as we predicted, but the position tripled. We went back and forth for 30 minutes. What about all these stocks that tripled after we sold them? That was certainly one mistake we have made and continue to make.

另一个错误是：对企业的评估失误以及自我欺骗。但所谓“无法脱手”其实是因为持股过多，而非真的无法卖出。

<!--en-->
Another mistake we have made: mis-assessment of a business and being in denial. But of denial was that we owned so much that we couldn't get out. It wasn't so much we couldn't get out.

只要买入价格合适，我们从不过分担忧流动性问题。如果我判断错误，就该为此付出代价。我们大量买入的那些公司所提供的流动性，足以弥补难以卖出的头寸带来的损失。只要时间足够长，最终总会奏效。

<!--en-->
We never worry too much about liquidity if I can buy it well. If I am wrong I should pay for it. Liquidity constraints in companies that we bought a lot of have more than paid for the ones we couldn't get out of. If you have a long enough horizon, over time it works.

**学生：** 您在小型股领域涉足甚多。您关注的公司/股票到底有多“小”？

<!--en-->
**Student:** You do so much in the small cap area. How small (are the companies, stocks) do you look at?

哥伦比亚大学商学院特殊情境投资课程

<!--en-->
Special Situation Investing Classes at Columbia University Business School

**JG：** 目前我们持有的典型投资项目规模都在数十亿美元级别。这也是投资小盘股的另一大优势，我想我之前提到过。擅长此道的人往往会变得富有，以至于他们不再关注小盘股，转而投向大盘股。因此总会有新的一批人加入。**在这里永远有起步的空间。** 我在书中也试图阐明这一点：并非小盘股本身更优。（小盘股在价格高低方面往往更容易被错误定价。）这也是学者们常犯的一个愚蠢错误……他们总会说：“嗯，你遗漏了这个因素，或者没包括那个因素……”

<!--en-->
**JG:** Right now the typical investment we own is in the multi billions. That is another great thing about investing in small caps which I think I mentioned before. The people who get good at this stuff, get wealthy so then they can't look at the small caps any longer. They go to the large caps. So there is always a new crop of people. **There is always room to start there.** I try to make it clear in the book too. It is not so much that small caps are better. *(Small caps tend to be more mis-priced both on the up and down side).*
That is another stupid thing that academics generally do.... They say.."Well, you left out this or you didn't include that......

我料想自己终将遭到攻击，因为学者们会说：“你没有剔除小盘股效应、低市净率效应。”他们试图剔除所有这些效应——但一旦剔除后，结果便与市场持平。关键在于：即便存在所谓的小盘股效应，其对应的股票规模也太小而无法购买。而小盘股效应之所以存在，是因为不受青睐的股票往往比普通股票具有更小的市值，且价格较低。

<!--en-->
I figure I will get attacked eventually because Academics will say, "You did not take out the small cap effect, the low price/book effect." They try to take out all these effects--but for that effect you equaled the mkt. But the point is that the small cap effect if there is one, they are too small to buy. But the small cap effect, if there was one, occurs because the stocks out of favor tend to have smaller caps more than the average stocks because their price is low.

我认为小市值股票的出现是因为它不受市场青睐。低市净率现象也是如此——股票之所以市净率低，只是因为它不受青睐罢了。它并非因为市净率低才显得便宜，这只是巧合而已，两者并存但并非因果关系。不能仅仅因为市净率低就认为它是好标的。与我所关注的指标不同——我看重的是股价相对于公司盈利水平的比例。在我看来，这更有意义；仅以低市净率来定价实在荒谬。

<!--en-->
I think a small market cap stock happens because it becomes out of favor. Same with low price book. The stock happens to have a low price to book because it happens to be out of favor. It is not cheap because it has a low price to book value. It is coincidental. It coexists. It is not a good buy because it is low price to book. As opposed to what this is--Rather than what I looked at--which was price relative to what the companies would earn. It makes more sense to me. It seems silly to me to just use low book value to price.

**学生：** 理论上讲，我们所供职的公司都是资本规模达数十亿美元的企业，因此我们不被允许购买市值低于4亿至5亿美元的公司。

<!--en-->
**Student:** Theoretically, the companies we work for will be firms that have billions of dollars of capital where we wouldn't be allowed to buy companies under $400 - $500 million in market cap.

## 本课程的目的

<!--en-->
*The Purpose of the Course*

**JG：** 本课程的核心在于为你提供进行估值工作的背景框架。你所做的无非是评估公司价值，并试图以更低价格买入。同时理解市场运作的背景与规律。短期内市场可能与你意见相左，但你必须坚持到底才能获得正确结果。

<!--en-->
**JG:** The whole point of this course is to give you a context in which to do your valuation work. All you are doing is valuing companies and trying to buy them for less. And then understand the context and how the market works over time. The market may not agree with you in the short term, but you have to stick it out to get right.

**你所做的只是评估公司价值并以更低价格买入。那么你所面对的全球背景又是什么？** 如果你评估的是大公司，那就计算其现金流。这与小盘股并无区别。并不存在什么明确的界限。大盘股往往是更成熟、更稳定的企业，因此它们并非单一产品公司。它们或许比小公司拥有更强的市场地位，但你仍可以考察相同的属性。也许大公司在一个细分市场中占据巨大份额。

<!--en-->
**All you are doing is valuing companies and buying them for less. And then what is the global context you are looking at?** If you are valuing large companies, then figure out the cash flows. It is no different than for small caps. There is no line drawn somewhere. Large caps tend to be better, more established companies, and therefore, they are not one product companies. They have maybe a stronger market position than small companies but you might look at the same attributes. It might be a small niche market that the large company has a great share in that market.

**无论我列举多少研究，归根结底还是关于如何评估公司价值。** 如果你能评估公司价值并以更低价格买入，同时具备“2+2=4”这样的基本认知，那就足够了——其余的可以忽略。如果你能买到那些长期盈利且价格低廉的好公司，你就能赚钱。这正是本课程的核心所在。

<!--en-->
**It is all about valuing companies no matter how many studies I blabber about.** If you can value companies and buy them cheaper and have the context to know that 2 plus 2 equals 4, then that is all you need--forget the rest. If you can buy good companies that are making money over time at a discount, you will make money. That is really what this course is about.

善于将事物置于具体背景中分析，这是我擅长的；而估值工作我认为自己只是中等水平。但我非常挑剔，只会选择自己能够评估的对象。我想你们所有人都能做到这一点，因为你们都在这里。

<!--en-->
Putting things into context which I am good at and doing the valuation work which I think I am average at. But I am very picky, and I pick the things I know how to evaluate. And I think all of you can do that because you are all here.

在大型企业中我可能会表现不佳，因为我对某个行业的判断未必优于他人——毕竟我不了解该行业的动态。但这是一种好的过程。如果你能掌握三四个行业知识……*琳达·格林布拉特*仅靠对零售业的了解便足以谋生。或者像制造业这样你从骨子里就熟悉的行业——这正是*沃伦·巴菲特*所说的“能力圈”概念。

<!--en-->
I might flounder at a big firm because my guess on a particular industry might be no better than anyone else because I don't understand the dynamics of that industry. But it is a good process. If you learn three or four industries. *Linda (Greenblatt)* has made a good living knowing one industry, retail. One industry you understand in your bones like manufacturing because that is your background. It is the *Warren Buffett* circle of competence concept.

*比尔·米勒*（Legg Mason Value Trust基金的基金经理）就是一个非凡的例子，他将自己的能力圈扩展到了常人不会关注的领域。他试图确定公司的真实价值并以更低价格买入。他努力去理解人们认为极其复杂的公司——比如*谷歌、亚马逊、eBay*。

<!--en-->
*Bill Miller* (portfolio manager of Legg Mason's Value Trust) is an extraordinary example is someone who has expanded his circle of competence to companies you generally don't look at. He is trying to figure out what a company is worth and buying it for less. He is trying to understand what people consider very complicated—*Google, Amazon, EBay*.

哥伦比亚大学商学院特殊情境投资课程

<!--en-->
Special Situation Investing Classes at Columbia University Business School

**学生：** 您会关注哪些要点呢？

<!--en-->
**Student:** What do you look for?

**JG：** 我总是在寻找资产价值与其交易价格之间的*差异*。那么我的替代方案是什么呢？由于目前我们持有一些大盘股，因此已全额投资。我担心负债累累的消费者群体。2000年我们也曾感到担忧——当时我们持有了许多盈利丰厚的公司股票，我们也知道互联网泡沫会破裂。标普500指数当时跌去了一半。我敢保证，这种事一生中不会经常发生。2000年我们的收益达到100%，但随后市场遭遇重创。现在的情况与此类似：我们已全额投资。如果我们发现其他更合适的标的，就会卖出现有持仓，因为我们不使用杠杆。

<!--en-->
**JG:** I am always looking for a *disparity* between what it is worth and where it is trading. Then what are my alternatives? Right now because we have some big cap stuff, we are fully invested. I am worried about the indebted consumer. We were scared in 2000 also. We owned a lot of companies earning a lot of money. We knew the Internet bubble would burst also. The S&P 500 dropped in half. There are not many times in your life that will happen, I guarantee it. We were up 100% in 2000 and the market got pummeled. That is sort of what we are doing now. We are fully invested. If we found something else we would sell something else because we don't use leverage.

## 杠杆

<!--en-->
*Leverage*

如果你打算成为高度集中的投资者，就不应使用杠杆。WEB说过，如果你只有一张包含20个选项的卡片，也能赚大钱。我会给你一张未来十年的“20孔打孔卡”，以帮助你保持纪律性。

<!--en-->
If you are going to be a very concentrated investor, you should not use leverage. WEB said you make a lot of money if you only had a 20 card punch card with 20 choices. I will give you a 20-hole punch card for the next ten years to help you be disciplined.

你不能使用杠杆，因为*你必须熬过市场低迷期*，这一点至关重要。

<!--en-->
You can't leverage because *you need to live through the downturns* and that is incredibly important.

从宏观角度看——我关注的内容包括：我的投资组合构成。这只是目前的练习而已。你的组合中有6只证券，且已100%投入资金。如果我们发现其他心仪的标的，就必须从中剔除一只。我们管理着一只基金中的基金。我们找到了一位来自*VIC*的基金经理。他管理的基金包含30只股票，因为他希望自己能安心入睡。但他很聪明，且拥有庞大的团队来发掘大量投资思路。他的见解是我们所没有的。

<!--en-->
Big picture--the things I look at: What I have in my portfolio. This is just practicing now. You have 6 securities in it, and you are 100% invested. Now if we find something else we like--it has to boot something else out of my portfolio. We run a fund of funds. And we found a money manager from the *VIC*. He ran a fund with 30 names because he wanted to sleep well. But he was smart and he had a big staff so he could source a lot of ideas. He had insights we didn't have.

我们想出了与他合作的方式。我们说：“听着，我们只想要你*最好的五个*想法，而不是30个。如果你想新增一个想法，就必须卖掉另一个。”你一次最喜欢哪五只股票呢？**我建议你采用6到9只股票的投资组合。这实际上是致富之道。**这是一种极具纪律性的策略：始终将最佳想法保留在投资组合中并集中投资。只保留最优秀的标的。WEB说他资金多于可投资的想法，但我觉得短期内你不会遇到这个问题。如果遇到，请来找我。

<!--en-->
We came up with a way to work with him. We said, "Listen we only want your *five* best ideas not 30. If you want to add an idea, you have to sell the other." What are your five favorite things at a time? **I would recommend to you a 6 to 9 stock portfolio. It is a way to get rich actually.** It is a very disciplined strategy to always keeping the best ideas in your portfolio and concentrate. Only keep the best things in your portfolio. WEB says he has more money than ideas, but I don't think you will have that problem for a while. If you do, please look me up.

**学生：** 您还会关注其他什么吗？

<!--en-->
**Student:** Is there anything else you look at?

**JG：** 有一点我们强调得不够，但它其实蕴含在我们当前的做法中——因为我们购买的是低价股票。要寻找**风险回报不对称的投资机会**。这是我们的行事准则。遵循安全边际原则，我们追求良好的风险回报比——即投入1元，可能获得5元回报。某股票价值10元，你可以5元买入，但该股价格也可能下跌。当然，你绝不会以50美分的价格买入大盘股。对于50美分的股价，我的看法是：“我会持有两三年，随着现金积累，它最终会值10元，而现在只需5或6美元就能买到。”这样的回报相当可观。有时这种情况会更快发生，市场会提前反映这些盈利预期。或许市场会比我更早察觉到这一点。

<!--en-->
**JG:** One thing we did not emphasize enough which is inherent in what we are doing because we are buying stocks cheap. Look for **asymmetrical risk reward investments**. It is inherent in what we do. Following the margin of safety principle we are looking for good risk reward-- a dollar down and five up. The stock is worth ten and you can buy it $5 but the stock could go down. You certainly are not going to buy a large cap stock now at a 50 cent dollar. The way I would look at a 50 cent dollar, "Well I am going to hold this for two or three years and in two or three years with the accumulation of cash it will be worth $10 but I can buy it for $5 or $6 now." That is a pretty good return. Sometimes it happens sooner and the market fast forwards those earnings upfront. Perhaps the market will recognize what I am seeing sooner.

有趣的是，我们经常与基金经理交流。我们能为他们提供的帮助之一，就是协助他们做出决策。**我们结识了一位人士，他仅用15年时间就将10万美元增值至2500万美元（15年复合年增长率达44.5%！），且从未引入外部资金。我们说服他为我们的基金操盘。**有一天，他分析了该公司的各项指标，发现其价值10美元，而股价仅为4美元。我们说：“你说得很有道理，听起来不错。”“还有一点，”他说，“他们刚刚决定将公司出售。”这对我来说听起来确实不错，对吧？

<!--en-->
It is interesting because we talk to our portfolio managers a lot. One of the things we bring to the table is that we can help the portfolio manager. **We met a guy who ran $100,000 in 15 years into $25 million (44.5% CAGR for 15 years!)** never running outside money. We convinced him to run money for us. One day he went through all the metrics of the company and it is worth $10 where the stock is trading at $4. We said, "Everything you said makes sense, which sounds great. "And one other thing," He said, "they just put the company up for sale." So this sounds really good to me. Right?

为什么你只在投资组合中分配7%而非20%给这只股票？如果你没有幸运地在2美元时买入，那么在4美元时你会大量增持吗？

<!--en-->
Why do you only have 7% of your portfolio in it instead of 20%? If you were not lucky enough to buy at $2 would you buy a hell of a lot more at $4 if you hadn't been so lucky?

他说：“我明白你的意思。”第二天，大量该股票被抛售，他便将仓位扩大了三倍。三周后，该公司以9美元的价格被收购。

<!--en-->
He said, "I see your point." The next day a big block of stock comes up in the stock and he tripled his position. Three weeks later the company is taken over for $9.

我所说的一切……人们指责我试图*把事情说得过于简单*。其实并非如此。当你看到这些结果（《魔法公式股票》在17年间分别上涨34%和22%）时，似乎显而易见。**但当你身处其中、经历那一年半的艰难时光时，却并不觉得如此明显。**我为何会被视为傻瓜？情况确实不同。回顾长期的累积数据或平均值时，说它显而易见且有效要容易得多。

<!--en-->
All the stuff I say...People accuse me of trying *to make it seem all too easy*. It really is not. When you look at these results (Magic Formula Stocks up 34% and 22%) over seventeen years, it seems obvious. **When you are****in the trenches and you are living through the year and a half and it sucks, it doesn't seem so obvious.**
Why am I an idiot? It is different. It is much easier to look at an accumulation over time or an average and say that it is obvious and it works.

哥伦比亚大学商学院的特殊情况投资课程：在投资组合管理中也是如此。存在诸如锚定效应、买入价格等心理因素，这些现象自然会发生。**我认为你的思维过程越清晰越好。也就是说：这笔交易值得做，我对自己的判断有十足的把握。你只需回归基本面即可。** 基本面就是市场最终会在三到四年内纠正错误，而你必须耐心等待。如果我错了，那只是偶尔为之；但如果经常出错，我就得另谋出路。或者我得找一个自己懂得如何估值的行业——这就是学习过程。最难的部分在于此。

<!--en-->
Special Situation Investing Classes at Columbia University Business School
The same thing in portfolio management. There is all the psychological things like anchoring, the price you pay. These things naturally go on. **I think the clearer your thought process, the better. Which is: It is worth this it is trading here, I have this much confidence in my opinion. You just keep going back to basics.** The basics are the market will get it right eventually in three or four years and I have to hang out. If I am wrong, I will be wrong some of the time. If I am wrong a lot of the time, I have got to find another line of work. Or I have to find some industry that I do know how to value and that is the learning process.
The Hard Part

**学生：** 最难的部分是什么？

<!--en-->
**Student:** What is the hard part?

**JG：** 我认为最难的部分在于将自己限制在那些能够算出其正常化收益的公司范围内。**我只选择那些我能算出——或容易算出——正常化收益的公司。**

<!--en-->
**JG:** I think the hard part is limiting yourself to those companies that you can figure out the normalized earnings. **I only limit myself to those companies I can figure out--or are easy to figure out--the normalized earnings.**

**学生：** 随着时间的推移，这种方法与您第一本书中的方法有何不同？

<!--en-->
**Student:** Over time what is the difference in this methodology compared to your first book?

**JG：** 这取决于不同时期的机会所在。直到20世纪90年代初，我才开始关注WEB所强调的好企业。我曾因投资糟糕的企业而吃亏。如果某资产价值10美元，而价格涨到12美元，那当然好；但如果跌至8美元，安全边际就会缩小。时间反而会成为你的敌人，而非助力。

<!--en-->
**JG:** It depends where the opportunities lie over time. I didn't get turned on to WEB's focus on good businesses until the early 1990's. I got burned in crummy businesses. If there is $10 in value and it is going to $12 then great, but if it is going to $8 then your margin of safety is degraded. Time is against you instead of working for you.

**学生：** 这张20孔打孔卡是用来进行20笔优质投资的吗？

<!--en-->
**Student:** This 20-hole punch card is for the purpose of making great 20 investments?

**JG：** 用打孔卡选出一半的投资组合标的。你填入10个想法，持有1到3年。随着年龄增长、节奏变慢且工作强度降低，我延长了持有期限并提高了集中度。

<!--en-->
**JG:** Put half your portfolio into stocks using your punch card. You put in 10 ideas and you hold them 1 to 3 years. As I have gotten older, slower and working less hard, I have extended my timeframe and increased my concentration.

我不知道你是否算过这笔账：你会用完这20个选项。这实际上更像是一种提醒——**少即是多**。你只能专注于最好的想法；如果觉得它不够好，就放弃。你的机会并非仅限于眼前所见。未来无法预知，但你的机会不在于购买当下最好的东西，而在于**等待可能出现的好机会**。当绝佳机会出现时，我确实会错失买入时机；有时会出现巨大机遇，这时拥有充足的现金储备就很重要。

<!--en-->
I don't know if you have done the math. You will use up your twenty picks. It really is more of a reminder that **less is more.** You can only focus on your best ideas. If you don't think it is great, then pass. Your opportunity set is not what is in front of you. The future is unknown. But your opportunity set is not in buying what is the best out there today, but **what might come along if you wait.** I am really losing an opportunity to buy when there is a great opportunity. There are times when there are huge opportunities and it is good to have dry powder.

我给你一些指标：你的门槛收益率应该很高，你必须非常有信心。全力押注于最佳机会。我所说的“全力押注”比大多数人都要激进——我们会将20%到30%的资本投入一个想法中。我们将股票持仓视为拥有一家优秀企业的部分所有权。

<!--en-->
I am giving you metrics--your hurdle rate should be very high, you should be really confident. Load up on your best opportunities. What I consider loading up is more than most people. We put 20% to 30% of our capital into an idea. We look at it (an equity position) as owning a piece of a great business.

我们之所以能发现好机会，是因为我们做了功课，并在不寻常的地方找到了它。“哦，它价格低廉是因为某个业务部门可能被关闭，届时其价值才会显现。”我们并非像发现谷歌那样偶然找到它。

<!--en-->
When we found a great idea was because we did the work and we found it in an unusual spot. "Oh, it is trading cheaply because this division could be closed down then the value will be revealed. It is not like we figured out Google.

还有两个问题，之后我们就休息。

<!--en-->
Two more questions and then we will take a break.

**学生：** 您是否已满仓投资？

<!--en-->

**JG：** 过去六个月里我们看到了很多好机会。

<!--en-->

我应该按兵不动吗？有时我们虽已满仓，但仍会继续寻找机会。你买入的股票下跌，卖出的股票上涨，但我已学会忽略这种痛苦。

<!--en-->
Should I have sat on my hands? Sometimes we are fully invested and are looking. The thing you bought goes down and the thing you sold goes up, but I have learned to ignore the pain.

这才是关键！当所有人都在考虑下个季度时，你必须**放眼两三年之后**。

<!--en-->
That is the key! You must think **two or three years out** when everyone is thinking about the next quarter.

#### 可比公司与估值

<!--en-->
*Comparables and Valuations*

一位学生列出了五种不同的价值类型：

<!--en-->
A student presented five different types of value:

* EV/EBIT，
* 市销率，
* 清算价值，
* 私人交易价值，
* 还有一两种其他指标。然后他对这五个数值取了平均值。我认为应该选择*一个*——更相关的指标。如果它们都在同一范围内，那倒无所谓；但单纯取平均值并没有太大意义。对于相对价值分析中的可比公司选择，我也持同样观点。很多人只是随便列出一堆可比公司。即便有些人做了ROIC和EV/EBIT分析并进行比较，那固然不错；但这仍比使用市盈率要好，因为市盈率会受到不同税收抵免等因素的影响。不过那八到十家公司未必真的是理想的可比公司。我仍会挑选出最相似的企业，仅针对两三家进行可比分析，而非取八到十家公司的平均值。我觉得这样反而更有用，而不仅仅是应付了事。有些公司确实找不到合适的可比对象，但**现金就是现金**，对此我的处理方式如下……你知道，我曾在*斯坦福·伯恩斯坦*向那里的年轻分析师们发表演讲（共50人）。*这在某种程度上既令人欣慰又令人难过*，但我确实经常收到这类问题。一位分析师举手问道：“我主要研究科技股。它们的估值方式与其他股票不同，我该如何对它们进行估值呢？”我说，*现金就是现金*，你是在评估其盈利流——它们都是绿色的。这取决于你的信心程度及其他因素。关键在于要具备*机构思维*，而他们至今仍沿用这种方式。*斯坦福·伯恩斯坦*是个很棒的地方。**你的优势之一就是能够*独立思考*。**哥伦比亚大学商学院的特殊情况投资课程：如果你找不到合适的可比公司，那就试着寻找具有类似资本回报率和增长前景的同类企业。*Rob Goldstein*（他的合伙人）在巴菲特收购可口可乐时，将*穆迪公司*与之进行比较，因为这两家企业有相似之处。虽有差异也有共性，但有个*基准*总归是好的。所以，如果在你所处的行业中找不到合适的可比对象，就找具有相似特征的企业进行比较。你要对那里的现金流及ROIC有信心。这就是我所追求的标准。多年来我们正是靠此赚了大钱，因为人们往往只以特定视角看待这个行业。不过，嘿，世事难料，但只要它能持续产生现金，或许就会被重新估值。看看这两个指标，它们很匹配。这家公司股价在25到30美元之间，另一家则在12美元左右。如果它们能持续赚钱，这种状况不会长久维持；你得等上两三年，但这是一种非常强大的模型——**用于在没有可比公司时找到参照物**。或者，以不同于传统的方式来分析某个行业。该行业内的公司或许定价合理，但有可能全部被低估。人们不习惯为……付费。过去人们只愿意为银行支付10倍的市盈率，但后来由于银行盈利能力增强且涉足更多业务，人们便愿意为其支付更高价格。如果难以找到可比公司，就找市场份额和前景相似的企业。

<!--en-->
* EV/EBIT,
* Price/Sales,
* liquidation value,
* Private transaction value
* and one or two others
Then he averaged the five. I say pick *one*—something that is *more relevant*. If they are all in the same range, it doesn't matter. Just picking an average doesn't mean much. I think the same thing with relative value—picking comparables. A lot of people just list a bunch of comparables. Even if some did the ROIC and EV/EBIT analysis and compared and that is good. It is much better than doing P/E ratios where there are different tax shields and everything else. But those eight or ten companies were not really great comparables necessarily. I would still pick out the businesses the most likely to be similar and do comparables on two or three companies instead of an average of 8 or 10. I think that might be more useful rather than just getting the job done.
There are other companies that don't have good comparables, but **cash is cash** and what I would do on that.....You know I gave a speech at *Stanford Bernstein* to the young analysts there (50). *It is kind of great and sad in a way* but I get these kinds of questions. An analyst raised his hand and said, “Well I do tech stocks. Those are valued differently than the others so how would I go about valuing them?” Well, I said, *cash is cash*, and you are valuing the earnings stream--they are all green. It depends upon your confidence level andeverything else. It is in the way you get into an *institutional mindset* and they are still doing it that way. *Sanford Bernstein* is a great place. **One of the advantages you have is thinking *straight*.**
Special Situation Investing Classes at Columbia University Business School
If you can't find a good comparable, then try to find a comparable business with similar metrics like returns on capital and similar growth prospects. *Rob Goldstein* (his partner) compared *Moody's* to *Coke* when Buffett bought it because there were attributes to those businesses that were similar. There were differences and similarities, but it is nice to have a *benchmark* of some sort. So if you can't find a good comparable within the industry of what you are trying to do, compare it to a comparable with similarities. You have confidence in those cash flows, the ROIC in that business.
So that is what I would look for. That is how we have made a lot of money over the years where people only view this industry a certain way. But, hey, things can change, but it is spinning out cash. Maybe it will get revalued. Look at these two metrics, they match up. This is trading at $25 to $30 and this is trading at $12. So that doesn't continue to last that long if they do continue to spit out the money, you have to wait two or three years, but that is a really, really powerful model **to find a comparable when you don't have one.** Or to analyze an industry a little differently than it has traditionally been analyzed. The industry might be efficiently priced relative to each other, but they all could be cheap. People are not used to paying for.........
People just used to pay only 10 times for banks, but then people started to pay more for them because they were earning more as businesses; they went into different businesses. If it is tough finding comparables find something similar in market share attributes and prospects.

## 零售商：

<!--en-->
*Retailer:*

他们说，过去五年的平均市盈率是这个数，或过去五年的最高市盈率是那个数，因此他们认为股价会回到这一水平。这有时并不合理，因为五年前该企业的增长前景可能截然不同。如今这家公司已入驻1000家商场，而五年前仅有400家；五年前它只在4个国家运营，现在则扩展至8个国家。该零售商的增长前景可能已经改变。

<!--en-->
They said, the average P/E over the past five years was this or the highest P/E over the last five years was that, and I think the price will go back to that. That doesn't make sense sometimes because the business could have been much different with different growth prospects back five years ago. Now the company is in 1000 malls and five years ago they were in only 400 malls. Five years ago they were in 4 countries and now they are in 8 countries. The retailer's growth prospects could be different.

仅仅因为股价会回归历史市盈率就说辞，就能看出这种逻辑上的漏洞。切勿掉入这个陷阱。

<!--en-->
Just to say it will go back to its historical P/E, you can see the flaw in that logic. Don't fall into that trap.

### 另一种传统思维的例子：戴尔公司

<!--en-->
*Another Example of Conventional Thinking: DELL*

来源：罗伯特·G·哈格斯特罗姆所著的《侦探与投资者：从传奇侦探身上学到的投资技巧》。在1992年至1994年这些关键的早期年份里，大多数关注电脑行业的投资者和分析师仍沿用旧有的假设。当时普遍的观点是：购买个人电脑制造商股票的最佳时机是其市盈率达到六倍时，而卖出时机则是市盈率达到十二倍时。这一直是历史上的交易模式，很少有人质疑它。华尔街大多数人的简单看法是：“这条经验法则在过去效果不错，何必改变呢？”

<!--en-->
From: *The Detective and The Investor: Uncovering Investment Techniques from the Legendary Sleuths* by Robert G. Hagstrom
In those critical early years of 1992 through 1994, most investors and analysts who followed computer companies were still operating on old assumptions. Conventional wisdom at that time held that the time to buy stocks of PC manufacturers was when the price was six times earnings, and the time to sell was when it hit twelve times earnings. That was the historical trading pattern, and few people saw any reason to question it. The simplistic view of most on Wall Street was, This rule of thumb has worked reasonable well in the past, so why change it?

“经济增加值”这一概念于1993年进入主流财经媒体视野，并登上了《财富》杂志的封面文章。任何仔细阅读该文的人都会得到一个重要启示：如果一家公司的现金收益能带来较高的资本回报率，那对其未来股价而言无疑是个好兆头。

<!--en-->
The concept of economic value added hit the mainstream financial press in 1993, with a cover story in Fortune. Anyone reading the article carefully would come away with an important message: If a company's cash earnings represent a high return on capital that should bode well for its future stock price.

此时，有思想的投资者本可以据此得出盈利的结论：我应该寻找那些盈利强劲且资本成本较低的公司。如果他们关注的是电脑公司，就会想到戴尔。

<!--en-->
At that point, thoughtful investors could have reasoned their way to a profitable conclusion: I should be looking for companies with strong earnings and low cost of capital. And if they were looking at computer companies, they would have hit on Dell.

教训是：既然戴尔的资本回报率很高且还在上升，作为投资者，为何要在其市盈率达到十二倍时就卖出呢？戴尔的经济模式建立在维持低资本成本的基础之上。什么是多余现金？哥伦比亚大学商学院的“特殊情境投资课程”指出：“在从企业价值中扣除现金之前，先了解企业的实际运营情况。”有些企业仅需少量现金即可运转；有些企业甚至使用负营运资本。我假定收购方并不需要这些现金，因此投资者最终能拿回这笔钱。零售商则需要储备大量现金以应对一两个销售淡季。有时，从企业价值中扣除现金的做法并不恰当——某些零售商必须在收银机中保留一定比例现金以满足顾客需求。总之，在扣除现金前，应先确定企业每年运营所需的现金量，例如：销售额的1%到2%。

<!--en-->
The lesson: Why would you, as an investor, sell Dell when it reached twelve (12) times earnings if its ROIC was high and going higher. Dell's economic model is built on maintaining low capital costs.
What is excess cash?
Special Situation Investing Classes at Columbia University Business School
**Understand the business before deducting cash from Enterprise Value.** Some businesses run with just a little cash. Some businesses use negative working capital. I assume the acquirer doesn't need the cash, so you would get it back then. A retailer has a lot of cash to weather a bad season or two. There are times that when you deduct the cash from Enterprise value, it is the wrong thing to do. Some retailers need to keep a certain percentage of cash in the til to accommodate customers. In summary, before deducting cash from Enterprise Value, determine the cash needed to annually run the business, for example: 1% to 2% of sales.

**基于企业价值的廉价分析：** 某股票价格为6美元，公司拥有5美元现金，预计两年后股价将涨至7美元。但你需支付6美元买入，而两年后股价仅升至7美元。企业价值翻倍（100%），但你的年化复合回报率仅为8%。此外，还要考虑管理层将如何支配多余现金。

<!--en-->
**Cheap on EV analysis.** The stock is at $6 with $5 in cash and the stock is going to $7 in two years. But you are laying out $6 and it is only going to $7. The EV doubles (100%) but your return is 8% annually compounded over two years. Also, think about how management will spend the excess cash.

## 漫威娱乐

<!--en-->
*Marvel Entertainment*

关于漫威有一篇精彩的报告，但我对其持保留意见。它被列为《魔法公式投资网站》的最新推荐之一。其分析思路还算合理：漫威先推出大片，随后通过授权角色赚取收入。他们确实拥有一批稳定的角色资源，因此业务具有一定的重复性特征。但问题在于：**何为“正常化收益”？** 未来几年可能会有两部电影上映从而带来相应收益，但去年只有一部电影上映。究竟应以每年两部还是一部电影来标准化计算收益呢？这种收益能持续多久？作者选取了每年1.5部电影作为基准。除非价格极其低廉，否则我可能会放弃这类投资。这确实是一桩不错的生意——品牌授权——不过要确定其正常化收益却并非易事。

<!--en-->
There was a great report on *Marvel*, but I struggled with that one. It is on the *Magic Formula Investing Site* as one of the recent picks. The approach taken was reasonable. You have a big movie, then they make money over the rights to the characters. They do have a stable of characters, so there is some *recurring* nature to the business with their characters, but the question is: **what are normalized earnings?** In a couple of years there will be two movies out and it will do this, but last year they had one movie out. Should you normalize at 2 movies or 1 movie a year. How long will it last? The person picked 1.5 movies per year. Unless it is super cheap, I might pass on something like that. It is a particularly good business—licensing brand names—however, I struggle in figuring out normalized earnings.

### 期权相关问题：股票仓位与期权仓位的权重分配

<!--en-->
*An Option Question: Weighting your position in Stocks vs. Options*

假设你发现了心仪的投资标的，那么应如何分配股票仓位与期权仓位的权重呢？

<!--en-->
Let us say you find something interesting, how much do you weight your position in options vs. a stock position?

**JG：** 这是个很好的问题。我的看法如下：如果我持有某股票30%的仓位，我认为这部分投资组合的风险其实有限，因为该投资对象是一家无杠杆公司。我将“灾难性下跌”定义为股价下跌33%（即占投资组合的10%——33% × 30%）。毕竟，当我决定买入30%的仓位时，买入价仅为内在价值的一半。比如我以5美元的价格买入，而我认为其价值应为10美元；即便股价跌至3.50美元或3美元，我所承担的风险也仅限于此。但若是期权……

<!--en-->
**JG:** That is a great question. This is how I would view it. If I had a 30% position in a stock, I don't think I am at risk for that 30% of the portfolio because the investment is in an unleveraged company. I view a disaster as being down 33% (or 10% of the portfolio—33% x 30%) because if I am going to be buying a 30% position I am buying it at ½ of intrinsic value. So I am buying at $5, and I think it is at worth $10. So I assume it goes down to $3.50 or $3. That is how much I have at risk. But with a leap...

投资股票的一大好处在于：从某种角度看，它们就像“永久期权”——除非公司破产，否则永远不会到期。因此，作为价值投资者，你可以放心等待：或许需要多花一年时间，但我相信股价终会回归公允价值，也许你不得不等待两三年。

<!--en-->
What is great about investing in stocks—one way to look at them—is that they are like *perpetual options*. They never expire unless the company goes bankrupt. So...the comfort you have being a value investor is it may take an extra year but I think it will get to fair value so I may have to hang out for two or three years.

然后你购买一个两年后到期的期权，这就把该选项排除在外了。我们有几笔类似的交易：包括一些股票以及两年期和2.5年后到期的期权。这样做会增加额外风险，因为世事难料——市场可能崩盘；房地产市场可能崩溃；消费者需求骤降；或者再次发生类似9/11的事件。我清楚从现在到未来五年间企业的发展方向——有点像沃伦·巴菲特的做法；我坚信在此期间企业会持续增长。企业的增长率会在7%到15%之间。我非常有信心在这段时间内企业能实现15%的增长。即便情况糟糕、中途出现大幅下跌，从今天到五年后企业仍会保持7%的增长率。

<!--en-->
Then you go buy an option that expires in two years you are taking that off the table. We have a few bets like that. We have some combination of stocks and some options that expire in two years and some in 2.5 years. You are adding another risk because stuff happens. The market could crash; the housing market could crash; the consumer drops dead; another 9/11. I know that if I draw a line from now until the next five years I know where the business will be—sort of a *Warren Buffett* thing; I feel very confident from here to there the business will grow and go up. The business will grow 7% to 15%. I feel very confident that the business will grow 15% during that time. If things stink and there is a big drop in the middle, it will still grow 7% from today until five years from now.

对于期权而言，其收益可能极不稳定，因此我会将这一点纳入考量。我把20%的仓位视为相当于40%的资金风险，也就是说该仓位直接承担了8%的风险。接着我再考虑时间因素（因为期权属于会随时间贬值的资产）；即便我判断正确，也可能因时机不对而受损。因此我将该仓位的权重从8%下调至5%。我假设自己可能会损失期权的全部投资金额。所以期权仓位在投资组合中的占比绝不会超过5%，而不会像股票仓位那样占到15%到30%。

<!--en-->
With an option, it may get very lumpy, so I take that into account. The way I compare a 20% position to risk 40% of my money so right away I risk 8% in that position. Then I take the time element (of a wasting asset), because I could get it right but have the timing wrong. So I take the position down to 5% from 8%. I assume I could lose *all* my money in my option. So an option position might not exceed 5% of my portfolio not 15% to 30% of a stock position.

我所说的“不杠杆”是指，这些投资无法让我输掉整个投资组合。赚钱时我看的是税前数字，亏钱时则看税后结果。比如，我在这项投资上亏损了50%，但税后实际亏损只有10%。其实有一些心理技巧可以运用。

<!--en-->
What I mean by not leveraging, is that they can't carry me away with my entire portfolio. When I make money I look at it pre-tax and when I lose money I look at it post-tax. Oh, I lost 50% on that but after-tax it was only 10%. There are little mind tricks you can play.

哥伦比亚大学商学院特殊情境投资课程

<!--en-->
Special Situation Investing Classes at Columbia University Business School

**学生：**您会购买实值期权还是虚值期权？您如何选择期权的行权价？

<!--en-->
**Student:** Do you buy in the money or out of the money options? How do you choose what strike price of an option?

**JG：**通常我会选择略为实值的期权。看涨期权或看涨/跳跃期权本质上等同于“买入看跌期权加上买入股票”；两者效果完全一致。一般来说，我不愿为看跌期权支付过高费用，所以我通常会选择较低的行权价——这样看涨期权的行权价也较低，从而削弱其中看跌期权的价值。行权价越低，我在看跌期权上的投入就越少。

<!--en-->
**JG:** Generally I buy a little bit in the money. A Call option or a Call/Leap is the same as **buying a put and buying a stock; they are identical to each other.** Generally, I don't want to pay a lot of money for the put so usually I would rather take a lower strike price where the Call strike price is struck at a lower price so the put option aspect of the Call is not worth as much. I am not investing as much money in my put the lower the price I go.

简而言之——另一种看待方式是考虑“风险与回报”。针对您的问题，有两种解读方式。其一是风险/回报关系。假设我持有IBM股票，当前价格为60美元，我的估值判断是两年半后其价格有望达到90美元。我可以花1美元买入行权价为75美元的看涨期权，从而获得15倍于投资的回报。或者我也可以说：“瞧，现在我能以9美元的价格买入行权价为55美元的看涨期权——它们处于实值状态；股票价格为60美元，购买该期权需花费9到10美元，但这10美元有可能增值到30美元，这样我的资金就能翻三倍；即便我判断错误，只要股价达到65美元，我就能收回全部投资。”我会把这些因素都考虑进去。如果我接近正确判断（即股价达90美元），就不太可能损失全部资金；要损失全部资金，股价必须跌至55美元。我会把这点纳入考量，但这并非精确科学。

<!--en-->
So bottom line—another way to look at it is your **risk & reward.** There are two ways to look at that in answer to your question. One is the risk/reward. Let us say I own IBM and it is $60 and I think my valuation thesis is that in two and a half years I think it has a good shot it can be worth $90. Ok? I can buy these $75 calls for a $1 for a 15 to 1 payoff. Or alternatively I could say, “Look, right now I could buy the $55 calls at $9—they are $5 in the money—the stock is at $60 and it is costing me $9 or $10 to buy that but that $10 can go to $30 so I triple my money and even if I am wrong I will get back all my money back if the stock is at $65.” So I will factor that in. It would be unlikely to lose all my money if I am close to right, because I am thinking $90. To lose all my money it would have to go to $55. I factor that in, but it is not a science.

**我向您展示的是：当股价为60美元时，我为何选择以10美元买入行权价为55美元的看涨期权，而非以7.50美元买入行权价为60美元的看涨期权？**这两种行权价哪个更好呢？我的做法是：“我总是关注看涨价差——即牛市价差策略。”具体做法就是买入行权价为55美元的看涨期权，同时卖出行权价为60美元的看涨期权。如果我以10美元买入55美元行权价的看涨期权，并以7.50美元卖出60美元行权价的看涨期权，那么净成本仅为2.50美元（10美元减去7.50美元，不含佣金）。若股价高于60美元，我最多可获利5.00美元，即100%的回报率。若股价恰好为55美元，我则损失100%。该价差的价值为5美元。若股价为57.5美元，我则刚好保本（55美元行权价加上为买入价差所支付的2.50美元等于57.5美元）。

<!--en-->
**The thing that I showed you was—how do I know to buy the $55 calls at $10 instead of the $60 calls at $7.50 when the stock is at $60?** Which is better of the two Call strike prices? What I say is, “I always look at the call spread—a bull spread.” What that involves is buying the $55 call and selling the $60 call. If I bought the $55 call for $10 and sold the $60 call for $7.50 for a net cost of $2.50 ($10 - $7.50, not including commissions). The most I can make if the stock is above $60 is $5.00 or a 100% return. If the stock is at $55 then I lose 100%. The spread is worth $5. If the stock is at $57.5, I am at break even ($55 Call Strike Price plus $2.50 paid for the call spread = $57.5).

如果股价高于60美元，那么2.5年后我的投资就能翻倍，因为我预计股价将达到90美元。根据我的分析，这听起来像是一笔不错的交易吗？我认为股价会达到90美元。所以我才会买入55美元行权价的看涨期权，因为这实际上等同于买入55美元/60美元的看涨期权价差。

<!--en-->
If the stock is above $60 it will be a double in 2.5 years because I believe the stock will be at $90. Does that sound like a good bet based on my thesis? I think the stock will be at $90. So I will buy the 55 call because I am effectively buying the spread of $55 call/$60 call.

当我想要直接持有某份期权时，我会在脑海中做这样的推算。我其实并不会真的购买价差合约。我究竟想持有55美元行权价的看涨期权还是60美元行权价的看涨期权呢？我通过在脑海中构建牛市价差来比较两者。多花2.5美元以10美元买入55美元行权价的看涨期权，相对于以7.50美元买入60美元行权价的看涨期权，实际上就相当于选择了牛市价差策略。

<!--en-->
It is an exercise that I do in my head when I want to own an option outright. I don't really buy the spread. Do I want to own the 55 call or the 60 call? So I compare the two by doing the bull spread in my head. By laying out an extra $2.5 to buy the $55 call at $10 vs. the $60 call at $7.50, I am effectively choosing a bull spread.

我最多能获利5美元，但该价差合约直到到期前都不会闭合。比如，我绝不会花4.5美元去购买。55美元行权价的看涨期权价值10美元，而60美元行权价的看涨期权只需7.50美元？**买入55美元行权价的看涨期权实际上就等同于持有该价差合约。**如果我买入55美元行权价的看涨期权，就等于同时为60美元行权价的看涨期权以及55美元/60美元的看涨期权价差付费。只需支出2.50美元，一旦判断正确就能获得5.00美元，即100%的回报率。不妨回家后在脑海里好好思考一下。

<!--en-->
The most I can make is $5 but the spread will never close until the end. I would never pay $4.5 for example. The $55 calls are plus $10 or lay out $7.50 for the $60 call? **Buying the $55 vs. the $60 is effectively like owning the spread.** If I buy the $55 call I am effectively paying for the $60 call and the $55/$60 call spread. Laying out the $2.50 brings me $5.00 if I am right for a 100% return. Just go home and think about it in your head.

**学生：** 既然通过期权能获得更高的回报，为什么还要去买股票呢？

<!--en-->
**Student:** Why would you ever buy a stock when you can get a higher return with an option?

**JG：**如果由于世界局势动荡，该股在未来两年内下跌8%，那么我持有该股票会损失8%，但持有期权组合则会损失100%的资金。

<!--en-->
**JG:** If the stock goes down 8% over the next two years because the world is a crazy place, I lose 8% in owning the stock, but 100% of my money owning the option spread.

问题在于，尽管我在这里告诉了你，但我还是经常犯错，因此这存在风险。如果这是一笔不错的赌注——我会把任何期权或价差头寸都称为赌注——那么从长远来看我会赢，但并非在每一次下注中都能如此。我希望成为那种赌场：只要我对这组赌注中所涉及公司的估值是正确的，就能随着时间推移赢得一系列赌局。

<!--en-->
The problem is that I am wrong a lot despite what I tell you in here so that is risky. If it is a good bet—and I would call any option or spread position a bet—I will win over time but not necessary on any one bet. I want to be the betting house where I will win a series of bets over time if my valuations of the companies in the group of bets are correct.

有人读过《财富公式》吗？这是一本新出版的书（见下方阴影框）。书中探讨了构建投资组合的最佳方式。**这本书讲的是赛马和赔率。** 如果你有不错的赔率，构建投资组合的最佳方式是什么呢？假设我抛硬币，正面朝上我能赚1美元，反面朝上则会损失0.5美元。你当然想频繁进行这种交易，但如果你有一大笔钱，也不会把100%的资金都押在这笔赌注上。即便这是一笔很划算的买卖，你也不会把所有钱都投入其中，因为可能会遭遇连败，从而输光所有钱财。

<!--en-->
Anyone read Fortune's Formula—it is a new book out (See shaded box below). It talks about the optimal way to structure a portfolio. **It is about horse racing and odds.** What is the optimal way to structure a portfolio if you have good odds? If I could flip a coin and I could get $1 if it is heads and lose $0.50 if it is tails. You want to do that a lot but if you have a pile of money you wouldn't put 100% of your money on that particular bet. Even though it is a great bet, you wouldn't put all your money into it because you could hit a bad run and lose all your money.

哥伦比亚大学商学院的特殊情况投资课程：从www.bankstocks.com开始。请解决以下问题。你带着1,000美元来到赛马场，看到某匹马在即将到来的比赛中获胜的赔率为5比1。你（仅你一人）与这匹马的训练师有秘密联络渠道，得知该马获胜的概率实际上远高于公布的赔率——比如为1/3。也就是说，你**比其他赌徒拥有实质性的信息优势**。你会用1,000美元中的多少钱来下注呢？

<!--en-->
Special Situation Investing Classes at Columbia University Business School
From www.bankstocks.com Solve the following problem. You're at the track with $1,000 in your pocket, and see that the posted odds on a certain horse winning an upcoming race are 5 to 1. You (and only you) have a secret line of communication to the horse's trainer, and learn that the horse's chances of winning are meaningfully higher than the posted odds—say, 1 in 3. Which is to say, you have **a material information advantage over other bettors.** How much of your $1,000 do you bet?

简而言之，这就是资本配置过程中最关键却最鲜被提及的难题之一。尽管CAPM理论的支持者大肆宣扬多元化的好处，但像沃伦·巴菲特这样的投资大师却深知其中门道。他们指出，多元化只能带来平庸的回报；真正的财富是在你拥有明显优势、能够把握那些罕见机遇时，投入大量资本才创造出来的。比如上面提到的那种赔率为5比1、出现概率仅为三分之一的机会。

<!--en-->
That, in a nutshell, is one of the most crucial and least discussed dilemmas in the capital allocation process. While CAPM types preach about the virtues of diversification, the Warren Buffets of the world know better. Diversification only assures mediocre returns, they point out; the *real* money is made **when you put a lot of capital to work in those rare opportunities when you have a true edge.** Like, say the 1-in-3 shot above that's going off at 5-to-1.

威廉·庞德斯通在《财富公式：击败赌场和华尔街的科学投注系统不为人知的故事》一书中探讨了这一问题。该书讲述了名为“凯利准则”的公式的历史。该公式能帮助赌徒（及其他资本分配者）在拥有信息优势的一系列投注中**最大化其利润**，同时又不会因下注过多而面临破产风险。以上述赛马为例：没错，为了充分利用你的内幕消息，你确实会想比平时下更大的注。但你绝不想把全部资金都押上——即便按你自己的判断，那匹马获胜的几率也只有33%。一旦破产，你就无法再重返赛场了。最佳的投注金额应介于两者之间。

<!--en-->
William Poundstone gets at this issue in *Fortune's Formula: The Untold Story of the Scientific Betting System That Beat the Casinos and Wall Street*. The book is a history of a formula called the **"Kelly Criterion"** that allows gamblers (and other capital allocators) to **maximize their profits on a series of bets where they have an information edge**, but without betting so much that they risk going broke. Take the horse-racing example, above. Yes, you'll want to bet more than you normally would, to make the most of your insider knowledge. But you don't want to bet everything: even by your own reckoning, the horse has just a 33% chance of winning. Once you're bankrupt, you can't get back in the game. The optimal bet size is somewhere in between.

凯利公式的命名者兼发明人名叫约翰·凯利，他是20世纪50年代和60年代贝尔实验室的数学家。凯利是在另一位贝尔实验室数学家克劳德·香农的研究成果基础上发展出这一公式的。庞德斯通指出，许多人认为香农是继爱因斯坦之后20世纪第二杰出的天才。尤其是，香农被誉为“信息论”之父，而信息论实际上为整个电子与数字革命奠定了**广泛的数学基础**。从集成电路到光纤电缆，再到DNA测序仪，所有这些技术都深深依赖于香农的研究成果。他的模型适用于任何形式的信息传输通道，无论是电子的还是其他类型的。这些模型帮助通信工程师最大限度地减少特定通道中的噪声——包括干扰、无用信息等等——同时最大化该通道所能承载的信息量。换句话说，香农本质上**找到了一种将不确定性转化为确定性的数学方法**。当然，对**区分信息与噪声**感兴趣的并不只有通信工程师；赌徒和投资者也同样需要这种帮助。因此，香农的一些数学理论能够在赛马场、21点赌桌以及华尔街派上用场，或许并非偶然。最早应用凯利公式的人之一是一位年轻的物理学研究生爱德华·索普，他将其与自己为21点游戏设计的算牌系统结合使用。（索普后来写了一本关于算牌的书，名为《击败庄家》，如今已被视为21点爱好者的经典之作。此后他还创办了一家极为成功的量化投资基金——普林斯顿-纽波特合伙公司；不过该公司最终在20世纪80年代卷入了鲁道夫·朱利安尼对迈克尔·米尔肯的追查行动之中。但那是另一个故事了。）

<!--en-->
The namesake and inventor of the Kelly formula is a man named John Kelly, a mathematician at Bell Labs in the 1950s and 1960s. Kelly developed his formula by building on the work of another Bell Labs mathematician, Claude Shannon. Poundstone says Shannon is considered by many to be the second-most-brilliant individual of the twentieth century, after Einstein. In particular, Shannon is the father of "information theory," which serves as the **broad mathematical foundation for essentially the entire electronics and digital revolutions.** Everything from integrated circuits to fiber-optic cable to DNA sequencers rely at rock-bottom on Shannon's work. His models apply to any kind information conduit, electronic or otherwise. They allow communications engineers to minimize the amount of noise—static, gossip, whatever—in a given conduit, and maximize the amount of information the conduit can carry. Which is to say, Shannon essentially **developed a mathematical way to convert uncertainty into certainty.**
Communications engineers aren't the only ones with an interest in **separating information from noise, of course.** Bettors and investors could use some help there, too. So it's perhaps not coincidental that some of Shannon's math can be put to use at the race track, the blackjack table, and on Wall Street. One of the first to apply Kelly's formula was a young physics grad student, Edward Thorp, who used it in conjunction with a card counting system he developed for blackjack. (Thorp later wrote a book on card counting called *Beat the Dealer* that's now considered a classic among blackjack aficionados. Later on he ran a hugely successful quant fund, Princeton-Newport Partners that eventually got tangled up in Rudolph Giuliani's pursuit of Michael Milken in the 1980s. But that's another story.)

你可能会问：凯利公式究竟是如何运作的？其实很简单。该公式指出，最佳下注金额是根据以下比例来确定的：

<!--en-->
How does the Kelly formula work, you ask? It's pretty simple. The formula says that the optimal wager size is determined according to the following fraction:

## 优势/赔率

<!--en-->
*Edge/Odds*

分母中的“赔率”是指赛马场投注板上公布的公众赔率。分子“优势”则是指：**如果你反复进行同样的投注，平均而言你能获得的利润数额。** 让我们回到第一段中的赛马假设案例，看看它是如何运作的。公布的赔率是5比1，因此我们将5作为分母。但请记住，你认为真实的赔率是1比3，而非5比1。如果你下注1,000美元，那么你有33%的概率赢得6,000美元（5,000美元加上你最初的1,000美元下注金），平均而言可获利2,000美元。在1,000美元的下注中，你的利润就是1,000美元——这就是你的*优势*。就公式而言，这1,000美元被记为1。

<!--en-->
The denominator, odds, is the public odds posted on the track's tote board. The numerator, edge, is the **amount you stand to profit, on average, if you could make this same bet over and over and over.** Let's go back to the horse racing hypothetical in the first paragraph, and see how it works. The posted odds are 5 to 1. So we'll put a 5 in the denominator. But recall that you believe the true odds are 1 in 3, not 5 to 1. If you bet $1,000, then, you'll have a 33% chance of winning $6,000 ($5,000 plus your original $1,000 wager), or $2,000, on average. On a $1,000 bet, your profit is thus $1,000. That's your *edge*. For the formula's purposes, the $1,000 becomes a 1.

哥伦比亚大学商学院的特殊情况投资课程 根据凯利公式，优势为1，赔率为5。代入数字后可得1/5。**你应该下注资金总额的20%。** 有几点需要说明：首先，这*仅在你拥有真正且实质性的信息优势时才有效*。如果没有这种优势，你的优势值就是零，因此不应下注。其次，只有当你绝对确定自己会赢时，该公式才会建议你全仓投入。在现实世界中，这种情况极少发生。因此，凯利公式能防止赌徒彻底倾家荡产，从而让他们在下一个机会出现时有资本继续操作。这绝非微不足道的好处。赌徒常用的其他资金分配策略，尤其是“马丁格尔策略”——即在输掉赌注后加倍下注以迅速挽回损失——往往会导致迅速破产。最后，将凯利公式应用于一系列投注，是复利增长最有效的方法。模型显示，比如更为激进的“凯利倍数2”策略实际上会导致*长期回报更低*。

<!--en-->
Special Situation Investing Classes at Columbia University Business School
So according to Kelly, the edge is 1 and the odds are 5. Plug in the numbers and you get 1/5. **You should bet 20% of your bankroll.**
A few comments are in order. First off, this **only works in instances when you have a true, material information advantage.** If you don't, your edge is zero, so you shouldn't bet. Second, the only time the formula will tell you to bet all you've got is when you're absolutely, positively sure you'll win. In the real world, that hardly ever happens. Thus Kelly prevents bettors from being wiped out completely, so that they'll have capital to put to work when the next opportunity rolls around. This is no small advantage. Other capital allocation strategies gamblers use, most notably “martingale,” in which the player doubles down after a losing bet in order to quickly recoup losses, can be quick trips to bankruptcy. Finally, using Kelly on a series of bets is the most efficient way to compound your winnings. Models show that, say, a more aggressive “Kelly times 2” strategy actually leads to *lower* long-term returns.

凯利公式的优势体现在各种投注策略的效果上；这些策略针对的是一系列假设的抛硬币游戏，其中投注者获胜的概率为55%。

<!--en-->
Kelly's advantages show the results of various strategies for betting on a series of hypothetical coin flips where the bettor has a 55% chance of winning.

当然无需多说，**经济学界对这一切几乎毫无用处**。首先，该公式是由数学家而非经济学家开发的，这自然让经济学家们持怀疑态度。其次，投资者能够拥有真正优势这一观点，与仍主导着大多数经济系的高效市场教条背道而驰。保罗·萨缪尔森尤其鄙视凯利公式（或在经济学界被称为“g”的公式），称其为一种“谬论”。

<!--en-->
It scarcely needs to be added, of course, that **the economics profession has roughly zero use for all this.** First off, the formula was developed by a mathematician, not an economist, which naturally makes economists skeptical. Second, the notion that an investor can have a true edge is anathema to the efficient-market dogma that still dominates most economics departments. Paul Samuelson is particularly scornful of Kelly (or “g,” as it's referred to in economics circles), calling it a “fallacy.”

凯利准则在经济学和MBA课程中几乎销声匿迹，这也解释了为何该公式在华尔街鲜为人知。其实这也不足为奇——要找到存在信息优势的机会本就极为困难。一旦这类机会出现，**投资者确实需要一切能帮助自己决定投入多少资金的工具**。尽管凯利公式或许不如在21点游戏中那般适用，但显然是个不错的起点。

<!--en-->
The Kelly criterion's virtual absence in economics and M.B.A. curricula explains why the formula is not well known on Wall Street. It shouldn't be. It is hard enough to find ideas where an information advantage is even possible. When those do occur, **investors can use all the help they can get** in figuring out how much capital to apply. Kelly may not be as ideally suited to Wall Street as it is to blackjack, but it sure seems like a good place to start.

A. It is uncertain and

### 穆迪公司案例

<!--en-->
*Moody Corporation Example*

**学生：** 您能详细讲解一下*穆迪公司*的案例吗？

<!--en-->
**Student:** Could you go over *Moody's* Example?

**JG：** 我花了很长时间才学会这一点，但希望传授起来不会太费时。假设当*巴菲特*买入*可口可乐*时，该公司年增长率是12%，而*穆迪*的年增长率也是12%，且两者每股盈利均为1美元。为了让*可口可乐*保持12%的增长率，它每赚1美元就需要拿出20美分用于再投资，以补充营运资金等。*可口可乐*用所赚美元的20美分来维持12%的增长，剩下的80美分则可用于其他用途。而*穆迪*要实现12%的增长却无需任何额外资金。因此我们说，相对于*穆迪*的1美元盈利而言，*可口可乐*的1美元盈利只相当于80美分。*穆迪*的盈利价值要高出25%（80美分对比100美分，即20美分/80美分=25%）。

<!--en-->
**JG:** This took a long time to learn but hopefully it won't take a long time to teach. Let us say, that when *Buffett* bought *Coke* it was growing at 12% per year and *Moody's* was growing at 12% and they both are earning $1 per share. For *Coke* to continue to grow at 12% it has to take 20 cents for every dollar and plow it back into its business for working capital, etc. *Coke* uses the 20 cents of the dollar they earn to continue togrow at 12% so the remainder is 80 cents for other uses. *Moody's* meanwhile needs $0 to grow 12%. So what we said was that a $1 from *Coke* is worth 80 cents compared to $1 for *Moody's*. *Moody's* earnings are worth 25% more (80 cents to 100 cents or 20 cents/80 cents for 25%).

哥伦比亚大学商学院的特殊情况投资课程：*穆迪*的1美元盈利比*可口可乐*的1美元盈利多出20美分（20/80美分=25%），即1美元对比0.80美元。或者说20美分/80美分，意味着*穆迪*的盈利价值高出25%。*可口可乐*最终的增长率会降至每年5%，因此它无需投入那么多资金就能实现5%的增长。8年后，它每年只需投入10美分便可维持5%的增长。所以*穆迪*的盈利价值并不会永远高出25%，可能只会高出10%左右。平均而言，*穆迪*的1美元盈利比*可口可乐*的1美元盈利高出15%。从长远来看，*穆迪*的盈利价值仅会比*可口可乐*高出10%，而非25%。我假设两家公司都永远保持5%的增长率，但*可口可乐*每赚1美元需投入10美分，而*穆迪*则无需投入任何资金。

<!--en-->
Special Situation Investing Classes at Columbia University Business School
The dollar of *Moody's* earnings was worth 20 cents more (20/80 cents = 25%) $1 vs. $0.80 for *Coke*. Or 20 cents/80 cents, so *Moody's* earnings is worth 25% more. *Coke* will eventually grow 5% a year, so they don't need to invest as much to grow at 5%. So 8 years from now they only have to invest 10 cents per year to grow at 5%. So *Moody's* won't be worth 25% more forever, it might be worth 10% more. So on average a dollar of *Moody's* earnings is worth 15% more than *Coke*'s earnings of $1. *Moody's* earnings would be worth 10% more not 25% over time. I assume both grow at 5% forever but *Coke* puts in 10 cents per dollar while *Moody's* puts in $0.

**JG：** 我认为这80美分会以一定速率增长。没错，要实现增长就需要更多的营运资金。在*穆迪*这类业务中，并不需要更多营运资金；但对于*可口可乐*，我假设它需要更多营运资金来支持增长。你提到的*穆迪*营运资金回报率超过100%这一点没错。确实，营运资金需要预先投入。我们参考历史数据来确定*可口可乐*和*穆迪*的再投资率。

<!--en-->

In that particular business (MCO) you don't need more working capital, but with *Coke* I assumed that you need more working capital to grow. Now you are talking about returns on working capital of over 100% for *Moody's*. Yes, you have to lay out for working capital. We looked at history to determine reinvestment rates for *Coke* and *Moody's*.

这么说吧，假设利率相同，那么我们就可以按此进行公平比较，并愿意为此多付15%。*可口可乐*曾达到某个价格水平，如今有所回落，但我们暂且不提它在上世纪90年代末的疯狂股价。不过在接下来的两三年里，*穆迪*的股价翻了三倍。我们拿两者作比较，是因为我们认为能在两三年内获得三倍回报。但别忘了，要留意其中的巨大差距。不要试图过度微调——如果你必须微调，说明你的投资逻辑还不够扎实。

<!--en-->
Look let us say interest rates were the same so apples to apples we can pay 15% more for that. *Coke* moved to some price and now it has come down, but let's ignore the crazy prices that it traded at in the late 1990's. But the next two or three years, the stock (*Moody's*) tripled. We are comparing the two because we thought we could get a triple in two or three years. But don't forget, remember the truck driving thought the huge gap. Don't try to fine tune it. If you have to fine tune it, then the investment thesis is a little too close.

别去理会*可口可乐*曾达到的疯狂股价——1998年时其市盈率高达65倍。

<!--en-->
Forget about the crazy price *Coke* traded at—65 times earnings in 1998.

去看看*达夫与菲尔普斯*在成长过程中有形资产的变化情况。其实并无变化，他们把每一分钱都用于股票回购。他们根本不需要额外资本来扩张。他们与*穆迪*非常相似。这是你所能见到的最优秀的商业模式。

<!--en-->
Go look at *Duff & Phelps'* change in tangible assets as they grew. There was no change, they spent every nickel on stock buy backs. They didn't need any capital to grow. They were very similar to *Moody's*. This is the best business you will ever going to see.

我首先举出*穆迪*的例子，是为了给你一个参照物。几乎所有其他企业都会逊色于它。相对于*穆迪*而言，一家企业的优劣程度如何呢？

我们最近研究了*美国运通*，并将其与*可口可乐*作了比较。它与*可口可乐*的相似度远高于*穆迪*。这是一种很好的比较方式，拥有这样的衡量标准很有帮助。巴菲特给学生的建议

Buffett's Advice to Students

**JG：** 我只想播放一段视频……一段*沃伦·巴菲特*对商科学生讲话的视频……

<!--en-->
**JG:** I just want to play one thing......... A video of *Warren Buffett* speaking to business students.........

**巴菲特讲座：** 在*所罗门兄弟公司*工作的*毛姆*从未谈及过薪水问题。他连续数月每天工作18小时。他对该向我汇报哪些事项的判断力令人惊叹。我常在给学生的演讲中引用这个例子：如果你们当中有人能挑选一位同学，从而分享其毕生的收入；你可以任选一人，且能获得此人终身收入的10%，那么你会考虑选谁呢？你会选择智商最高的人吗？或是成绩最好的人吗？恐怕不会。**你考虑的是一系列品格特质。** 这些特质都是*可以培养的*。你不会去想谁能把橄榄球扔出65码远。*本·格雷厄姆*记录下了他所欣赏的他人特质以及他厌恶的特质。这些特质都是你可以选择的。**习惯的枷锁轻到难以察觉，直到它们重到无法挣脱。** 那些你希望养成的好习惯，正是你希望从他人那里获得10%收入的原因。我发现那些表现出色的人并非拥有最强动力，而是拥有*最高效的动力系统*。正是这些品格特质最为重要。清单左侧的优良品质是我自己无法具备的，而右侧的不良品质是我自己无法摆脱的。最终，你要决定成为那个值得别人购买其10%收入的人。

<!--en-->
**Buffett Lecture:** *Maugham* at *Salomon Brothers* never once spoke about salary. He worked 18 hours days for months and months. He showed uncanny judgment on what to bring up to me. I often use this illustration in my talks to classes. If one of you could pick one of your classmates in order to share in their earnings for the rest of their life. And you could pick anyone you wanted and you would get 10% of their earnings of that individual for the rest of their life, what would you think about in terms of whom you picked? Would you think about the person with the highest IQ? The highest grades? Probably not. **You are thinking about a whole bunch of qualities of character.**
Every one of those qualities is *attainable*. You are not thinking about who can throw a football 65 yards. *Ben Graham* wrote down all the qualities that he admired in other people and the qualities that he found objectionable. Those qualities are ones that you can choose. **The chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too heavy to be broken.** The right habits that you would want to obtain of someone you would want to own 10% of their earnings. The people I see who function well are the ones who don't have the biggest motors but the *most efficient motors*. It is those qualities of character that are most important. What on the lefthand side of this list (good qualities) I can't achieve myself and what on the right hand side of the list I can't get rid of myself (bad qualities). In the end decide that you will be the one you would buy 10% of.

哥伦比亚大学商学院的特殊情况投资课程：想想看，真正能把这点记在心上的人有多少——尤其是商界人士。我认为你们都能变得非常出众。你们都具备能力与智慧。只要始终努力做正确的事，你们就能以多种方式取得巨大成功。我很享受给你们授课的过程。掌声响起。结束。

Think how few people actually keep that in mind—think of those in the business world. I think you can all be very special. You all have the ability and the intelligence. You can decide to be very successful in very many ways by trying always to do the right thing. I enjoyed teaching you.
